utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone in this courtroom after a long time. Before I continue, General Galic, is the translation functioning properly?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When I said "after a long time," I have to add to that that the Chamber should apologise for not having seen you within 120 days from the last time we saw each other. We are today in a Status Conference. Usually on Status Conferences we'll deal with matters of health and detention conditions and whatever other subject the parties would like to raise. May I first ask Prosecution and Defence first of all, because I've forgotten that, too, to give their appearances and then indicate whether there's any other subject we should deal with apart from the ones I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour, Mark Ierace for the Prosecutor. Nothing to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. On behalf of the Defence, as lead counsel, my name is Mara Pilipovic, my colleague Stephane, and our case manager Aleksandar Momirov. The Defence has decided to raise a few matters, and my learned colleague Stephane will raise them. As for the condition of health of General Galic, you have already said that we will be discussing that, and I think that General Galic will give you some additional information about his health himself though we have visited him and talked to him over the past few days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When you are referring to co-counsel as "Stephane," I take it that you refer to Mr. Stephane Piletta-Zanin, co-counsel in this case. If there is any need, especially if it comes to health, to go into private session, I may invite the Defence to indicate when that will be needed so that we can discuss matters, if necessary, not in public but in private session. Talking about the agenda, at the end of this hearing I will give an indication of at least an expectation when the judgement will be delivered. I can imagine that that would be one of the questions of the parties as well. Ms. Pilipovic, would you indicate which issues you'd like to raise and whether you'd rather start with health and detention conditions or whether you'd first like to raise the other issues you have in mind. Or Mr. Piletta-Zanin has in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I believe that mentioning my first name, Ms. Pilipovic indeed referred to me, and I think that we keep Mr. Galic's statement for the end because that is the general custom, for the accused person to address the Court at the end, and I think that this rule should be applied here. And if you're giving me the floor, I would like to raise two matters to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. President, there is a problem that arises. I wrote this morning -- actually, I wrote it yesterday, the mail that I'm sure you received a copy of today, and I address myself to Mr. Ierace, asking that in this case, when we had very late disclosure of documents, I think this is one of the very rare cases when the Prosecution disclosed documents not only after the end of its case but at the end of the proceedings, I am wondering how we can have guarantees, not just by Mr. Ierace, that the Prosecution doesn't have other documents that may be considered exculpatory and which the Prosecution should have provided us with in a timely manner for us to be able to defend General Galic properly. What we need is information, clarifications, and guarantees. I repeat that from the very beginning, we were reproached because we said that we are running the risk if we do not fully keep track of the computer documents, and we were proven to be right to some extent because some documents appeared later on. So how can we know clearly that we have no more documents to disclose -- that is, that the Prosecution, rather, has no other documents to disclose? The other point, Mr. President, is one that I would say was far more fundamental. You will remember that we -- when we pleaded at the time, I think that I myself said that history unfortunately shows that there are situations that are comparative to what we had, and we were in a sense a kind of laboratory. I'm referring to Iraq. And I think that today, five or six months since the last hearing, there is more and more reliable information provided by the media regarding the number of civilian victims in Baghdad and Basra and other Iraqi towns within the framework of operations engaged in by the coalition and which generally speaking are not considered to be a coalition of the axis of evil. And these figures are most instructive, and it is clear that from a historic point of view, we have to take into account those figures, because in a few weeks of combat, there were more civilian victims than there were in Sarajevo as a whole. That's all I wanted to say. It's not to plead but simply to draw the attention of the Chamber to these facts. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that you raise two issues. The first one is you would like to get an assurance from the Prosecution, I take it, that they take their ongoing obligation to disclose whatever might be exculpatory serious and you would like to have this confirmed today. Is that correct? Mr. Ierace, could you give a confirmation that under your ongoing obligation to disclose whatever material that might be exculpatory that there's nothing you have to disclose at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can't guarantee that there will not be further disclosures. Indeed, perhaps in the next week. The Prosecution takes very seriously its obligation imposed by Rule 68 that the existence of material known to the Prosecutor, and I emphasise the next few words "which in any way tends to suggest the innocence or mitigate the guilt of the accused must be disclosed." In other words, not material which is exculpatory but which in any way tends to suggest the innocence. That is a very broad ambit. The Prosecution assiduously filters through material which comes to it with that in mind. The Defence has received a quantity of material which has been generated since the trial was completed in May, and it has also received material which came into possession of the Prosecution before then, and that I regret. With the hundreds of thousands of documents that we have to go through, it sometimes happens that we become aware of material which has been in our possession for some time which is caught by that extreme test. Mr. President, as you are aware, there is another trial taking place at the moment which is canvassing the same issues as this trial, and as you might well imagine, that involves further investigations and further material coming to light. In terms of further disclosure, with that in mind I might point out that under the Blaskic Appeals Chamber decision, it seems the Prosecution is obliged to serve upon the Defence the transcript of evidence given by witnesses in that trial where the witnesses are the same as those who gave evidence in the Galic trial. And beyond that, there are some other witnesses who didn't give evidence in the Galic trial who have recently given evidence in the Milosevic trial. It seems we must serve that material on the Defence even though it's open source. So for that reason alone, I anticipate there will be some further disclosure. I can assure you that as soon as decisions are taken, that material is caught by Rule 68, then it is disclosed. And if it's material that we've had available to us for some time, not only in that circumstance is it disclosed to the Defence, but it is also disclosed to the Bench. Mr. President, I don't understand the second point raised by Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that is where he referred to Iraq and press reports and so on. Perhaps that might be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Ierace. If I do understand your response, it is that you take your ongoing obligation under Rule 68 seriously, and you point specifically at developments that are still ongoing and that might influence your duties under the ongoing obligation. Then the second issue, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I do understand that you consider it of importance to draw the attention of the Chamber to what you say appeared in press reports on the present situation not within the territorial jurisdiction of this Chamber. Are there any other issues, apart from the ones I mentioned, to be raised at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a point of clarification. I think that we cannot begin again as we did recently, that is disclose documents, be requested to review them to see whether they are or not of an exculpatory nature, et cetera. I wish to underline one thing, and that is that the Prosecution had a large portion of the documents disclosed to us, if not all of them, in their possession even before the closing of its own case. Therefore, I think that the Prosecution cannot say this, "I'm sorry it was in the right-hand drawer and I looked in the left-hand one," and then the other way round. I think a deadline must be set for the Prosecution for it fully to empty its sack - I apologise for the expression - and then we can go on. We cannot wait endlessly, waiting for other proceedings to construe the effects on this case. I think that would be quite inappropriate, and the Defence is objecting vehemently to such proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber expects the Prosecution to disclose whatever it has to disclose and takes it that any material in the possession of the Prosecution where the Prosecution is aware after having taken all measures to become aware, if possible, are disclosed. So therefore, there's no need to set a date specifically not because it's difficult to set a time limit for an ongoing obligation. Then I turn to you, General Galic. Would you like to give your position on your health situation in the Detention Unit in private session, or would you rather do it in open session?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, and with your permission, I would like to say a few words about the question raised before this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I believe that it is not a good idea for my Defence counsel to receive new material and not to be able to consult with me, and they have to respond to those materials. Consultations by telephone, if I don't see the documents myself, are rather superficial. So I would request that that does not happen. In other words, that the Defence be allowed to come and see me in the Detention Unit, to show me the documents, for me to review them together with them, and only then for them to respond to you as the Chamber or to whoever it is they have to respond to. That is the first point. Secondly, I think that there are several matters of significance, and I believe that the Prosecution or, rather, Mr. Ierace does have access to those materials which, in my opinion, would be mitigating. The Defence has requested some of those documents, but I would mention some of them. First of all, in June 1992, I asked to be retired. This request of mine, and it is well known that it was -- that UNPROFOR seized all the documents of the 1st Krajina Corps from Banja Luka, and it was to that corps that my request was addressed, and I think that document must be somewhere there. Secondly, the Defence asked the Prosecution to show them what mixed military commissions were doing. According to my knowledge, these mixed military commissions were formed on the 21st of December, 1992, upon the proposal of General Simpson, the Chief of Staff of the UNPROFOR command for Bosnia and Herzegovina and an envoy of Lord Owen's. Several such mixed commissions were formed at the time. One of those is the one that I am interested in. I know that there was also a subcommission which worked only on Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 22025 to 22027. the basis of assignments given to it by the mixed military commission, which means, according to my knowledge and information given to me, they had meetings at the airport mostly representatives of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, whether it be General Mladic, General Gvero or General Tolimir or someone else. So I would kindly ask those documents to be reviewed, that is, to see what those commissions were meant to be doing. In my opinion, they were supposed to be doing the things that I am being charged with, that is, to deal with the incidents between the armed forces. I never spoke to the enemy side, that is, with representatives of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I never met with them throughout the war. It was these gentlemen who attended those meetings. So I would request that if such materials exist, that they be disclosed. That is with respect to the first issue. With your permission there are some other points but I don't want to tire you today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I stop you for one second, General Galic. This is a Status Conference. That means that this is not the place to discuss, apart from the trial has been closed, but to discuss any content of material or information. I therefore do understand the observations you just made, that you are specifically pointing at some documents, some documentation of which -- which you consider certainly to be within the scope of Article 68 and, therefore, you ask the specific attention of the Prosecution to again look at whether these documents are available or not. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Might I respond briefly to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The two specific types of documents that the accused has referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Madam Pilipovic indeed did request from us any documentation we had of the Mixed Military Working Group, and they were provided to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Most recently approximately 12 months ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: During the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So whatever you had in your possession in respect of these type of documents they were disclosed to Miss Pilipovic, as far as I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic is nodding No. Could perhaps, since this is not an issue that could be easily solved at this very moment, if Mr. Ierace says that he disclosed something and you say it was not disclosed, that you meet and try to clarify that, because I couldn't say who of you is giving the proper information.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have a reply, that is the letter from my learned friend in response to the request of the Defence for those documents, and in this letter it is stated that those documents don't exist. I can check that out, and we can meet on that matter, but I have not received a single document with respect to these Mixed Military Working Groups. There's only a single minutes or record that General Galic is aware of. I received that from the Prosecution. But in any event, I will be only too glad to consult with my learned friend over this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me make one thing quite clear: A Status Conference is not a hearing on a motion to reopen the trial. So therefore, I did understand you well, General Galic, that when we are speaking about disclosure that you have drawn specific attention to certain documents and that there seems to be some disagreement on whether they have been disclosed, whether they do exist or not, and I would rather not, on the basis of this oral information, further enter into a debate on this issue. General Galic, you said that you had other points you'd like to raise. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked for your permission to comment on the first issue, and I felt I needed to comment, though I would have more to say. But as it is a Status Conference, I only focused on matters that are known already. Regarding my state of health, I think that is one of the questions we can address. Thank you for showing your interest at each Status Conference and during trial, too, and I appreciate your consideration and attention regarding my health, because after all, the trial lasted 220 days, which is not a short period of time. And in spite of my health, I managed to endure. But it is interesting that no one ever asked me why I came to be in such a condition, when did that condition set in. I don't know, Mr. President, whether you wish me to explain that today or perhaps you're already familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that I am familiar with it to the extent necessary. The issue and whatever consequences it should have is a matter that could have been raised at trial, and of course I'm aware that it was at a specific occasion that you -- that you -- that you consider that your health condition deteriorated suddenly. At this moment, I'm mainly interested to know whether there is any significant change in your health situation, and the Chamber has, during the whole of the trial, been aware that you were suffering especially from pain in your back. And the Chamber has always very much appreciated that even at moments where it was difficult for you to sit longer, that you always showed great cooperative attitude. But if there is anything that changed or if there's anything new you would like to inform me about, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should only like to say that it was not only a peculiar situation. It was a case of overstepping of authority. I was commander in military police for five years, so I know what powers military police have. I was a commander in the army for 30 years. I know what powers military men have. And I was arrested by the UNPROFOR at a time when my indictment was sealed, and I know all the things that have been done to me, and that is why I have a stiff back. I'm suffering from consequences. I now have no teeth. One of my teeth was knocked out, although two were in the danger of being lost. I suffered surgeries. One of my legs was saved by therapy, and now I have problems with my spine. I can tell you that the administration of the Detention Unit, as it seems to me, did everything in their power. I visited the Bronovo hospital - I believe that's the name of the hospital - and the neurosurgeon there told me that I have two options: I can undergo therapy and suffer a little or undergo surgery. I opted for therapy involving medication and physiotherapy that is available to me at the Detention Unit, and to some extent that helped. But then I was sent to see a neurologist, I believe -- I hope I'm not mistaken. I think it is a neurologist, because we are never told the exact profile of the specialist we are going to be seen by. They are always very courteous; they shake hands, they ask questions, and I can say that they are really humane and nice people. That second doctor told me I did not need surgery, that my problem can be treated by traditional therapy, and he changed my medication. I'm talking about what happened a month ago now, Your Honour. But my condition deteriorated significantly so that right now, I cannot cover a distance of 100 metres even, and it is very difficult for me to even stand. I need rest after the slightest effort, my leg goes to sleep, my right leg goes to sleep, and then the pain goes onto my left leg. The pain grew worse over the past ten days so that my dosage of medicine was doubled, but even that does not seem to have any effect. I still suffer great pain, especially when I walk. For a while I had trouble sleeping, and in those ten days, I lost seven to ten kilos, which might not be such a bad thing. But you must believe that this is affecting me both physically and mentally. As for the prospects, they promised me -- and I'm now trying to only inform you -- they promised that they would give me injections that are called blocks, blocking pain, blocking those sections of nerves which lead towards the leg, and the downside of this is that it can lead to further deterioration in the future. So the only thing that remains for me is to see how these injections will work. But very briefly, I'm having a very bad time. I don't know whether that's right or wrong, but all the others that I know of with similar problems went somewhere else for such surgery, outside of Holland. Another matter is the way therapy is administered at the Detention Unit. In one case that I'm familiar with, a man had his wound washed with tap water. So I am really not looking forward to undergoing surgery right here. And if you need more information, I would gladly provide it in the form of a statement or whichever way you tell me to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, General Galic. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are familiar with the shortcomings of the Defence, and the Defence wish to say that on page 13, line 2 of the English transcript does not reflect the reality. The doctor that General Galic consulted didn't say that he would just suffer a little, but on the contrary, that he should suffer, that he would suffer. So the word "little" in the transcript was not pronounced by General Galic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Just for clarification, General Galic, Mr. Piletta-Zanin draws our attention to the fact that you were given the choice either to suffer or to undergo surgery, so to suffer while being treated or undergo surgery; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Basically, yes. To suffer, to tolerate pain combined with therapy, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I was told by the first doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. General Galic, unfortunately or fortunately, I have no jurisdiction over doctors, so whatever they do or do not is beyond my competence, and I'm sorry to hear that what has certainly been intended as to improve your health situation turn out to be -- to deteriorate your health situation. You know the position of the Chamber. If there's any issue where the Chamber's interference would be needed because you're not properly treated and if this would have an impact on you and on your case, then we certainly will, as we did before, interfere. Of course we cannot cure you, and I do not know whether doctors will be able to do that, but it's -- I do understand how difficult it is to get new treatment and then feel worse than before and then to see that all kind of other new medicaments are needed in order to try to get you back to at least the situation you were in. Unfortunately, I cannot change that. As I said, we have no jurisdiction over doctors, and I don't know whether it would do any good to your health situation if we would have. You -- in passing you also mentioned something about the Detention Unit, the way they are washing wounds. Is there any other issue in respect of the Detention Unit you would like to bring to our attention?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, nothing in particular, perhaps just one detail that affected me yesterday, although perhaps now is not the best time, but I'll try to describe it for you. The latest news in the Detention Unit is that nowadays when they are taking us to the infirmary, they are binding us, tying our hands with handcuffs, but the handcuffs they're using look very much like the shackles used when a person is taken from death row to execution. It's the kind of thing that is like shackles, about 15 centimetres thick. They're made of plastic, about 10 centimetres wide, and when you put your arms alongside your body, I felt like being taken to the electrical chair. I don't know whether everybody has the same impression, but it was very unpleasant for me, and I really didn't like it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You know that security is primarily the responsibility of the Registrar. I will ask Madam Registrar to pass this part of the transcript to the Registrar so that he is informed about your observations. Is there anything else you'd like to raise?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if you're asking my opinion, we are already in the Detention Unit. I really am not sure how necessary it is to be -- we are driven by armoured vehicles. It's not necessary where I am concerned. I know that much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand, but this again is security issue that is the responsibility of the Registrar primarily, but I take it that transportation over Dutch territory is also a joint -- a joint concern of the Netherlands government and the Registrar. Is there anything else one of the parties would like to raise? If not, I will make -- I express as the expectation of the Chamber, but of course I'm a bit troubled by what has been said about disclosure, but if I would ignore that, it would be the expectation of the Chamber, and I'm saying an expectation because a Scheduling Order still will have to follow, to deliver judgement on the 5th of December. That then concludes this Status Conference.
